narrative:
The model determined that you have a 95% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the law school uses this prediction to decide admissions, your application was rejected.

The three factors that most strongly influenced this outcome were your LSAT score, your class ranking in the third year of law school, and your first-year class ranking. All three pushed the prediction heavily toward failure.

Your LSAT score of 18 was far below the average of 37 among students who were accepted, and this was the single strongest reason the model expected you to struggle on the bar exam. Your third-year ranking in the bottom decile (compared to an average around the middle of the class for accepted students) was the second most important factor and further increased the predicted risk of failure. Your first-year ranking, also at the very bottom of your class, added additional weight in the same direction.

These academic performance signals were so strong that the model was confident you would not pass the bar on the first try. Your family income, gender, race, planned full-time status, and undergraduate GPA played no meaningful role in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your standardized test skills and academic performance. Consider retaking the LSAT, enrolling in a structured bar-preparation course, or strengthening your study habits before reapplying. Demonstrating clear improvement in these core areas will be the most effective way to change future predictions. (248 words)
